title: Refrigerator temperature log: how to keep one and avoid fines
excerpt: Record readings at least twice a day, set limits for each type of equipment, and act when readings fall outside the limits. Inspectors look at the response, not just the numbers.

body.text: The rule is simple: record refrigerated-equipment temperatures at least twice a day, usually in the morning and evening. In practice, that may not be enough: if a refrigerator breaks at lunchtime, the evening reading will only record products that have already spoiled. A good practice is therefore to take three readings and add an automatic sensor.

items: Refrigerator for raw ingredients: 0…+6 °C (depending on the product).
Display case for cold dishes: no higher than +14 °C.
Heated display case: no lower than +65 °C.

body.title: If you use a sensor
body.text: A wireless sensor that records data to the cloud takes a reading every 5–10 minutes. The journal is generated automatically, and deviations are not lost between shifts.
What to do when there is a deviation

items: Record the event in the journal: time, reading, and who noticed it.
Check the products: if the temperature was above +5 °C for more than 2 hours, reassess their organoleptic properties and shelf life.
Complete a CAPA: record the cause (power outage, open door, or compressor failure), what was done, and who is responsible.
If a product is disposed of, record the write-off and identify the batch.

body.text: What matters to an inspector is not “perfect” temperatures, but evidence that deviations are addressed. A reading of +7 °C with a note saying “detected, product disposed of, compressor serviced” shows a working system. By contrast, +4 °C every day for a week without a single variation looks suspicious.
